title: From Training to Deployment: Post-Hoc Causal Feature Identification via Sensitivity Ratios

5.1 RQ1: Operating Regime and Failure Modes


Figure 1: RQ1: NSR AUROC as a function of KK and ε\varepsilon (30 seeds per
cell). K=2K=2: identically zero (Theorem 4.3(ii)). K≥5K\geq 5,
ε≥1\varepsilon\geq 1: AUROC =1.000=1.000 with zero variance. KK acts as a
binary threshold, not a continuous dial.


The theory makes four precise predictions: NSR is identically zero for K=2K=2
regardless of shift magnitude; it achieves reliable separation for K≥3K\geq 3 with
sufficient shift; it collapses as O​(ε4)O(\varepsilon^{4}) near the noise floor; and
degenerate geometry can make K=3K=3 behave like K=2K=2. We test all four on
controlled shift schedules across K∈{2,3,5,10,20,50}K\in\{2,3,5,10,20,50\} and
ε∈{0.05,…,5.0}\varepsilon\in\{0.05,\ldots,5.0\}. Full details are in Appendix A.8.

Operating regime. The K×εK\times\varepsilon AUROC heatmap
(Figure 1) reveals a sharp phase transition.
At K=2K=2, NSR^j=0\widehat{\operatorname{NSR}}_{j}=0 exactly for all jj and all ε\varepsilon
(AUROC =0.500=0.500), confirming the algebraic cancellation of
Theorem 4.3(ii). For K≥3K\geq 3 and ε≥1.0\varepsilon\geq 1.0, AUROC
=1.000=1.000 with zero variance across all 30 seeds, with NSR values for causal
features lying in [1.2×10−4, 2.9×10−4][1.2\times 10^{-4},\,2.9\times 10^{-4}] irrespective of
ε\varepsilon, exactly the finite-sample floor predicted by
Theorem 4.2(ii). The role of KK is threshold-like: once
K≥5K\geq 5, increasing it further shifts the transition ε\varepsilon by at most
one grid step.

Degenerate geometry. Theorem 4.3(ii) predicts collapse not
only when K=2K=2 but whenever shift magnitudes are symmetric. Table 1
tests six exact configurations. Symmetric shifts (β=[0,1,−1]\beta=[0,1,-1], K=3K=3)
give population NSR=0\operatorname{NSR}=0 for all features; empirically, AUROC =0.584±0.238=0.584\pm 0.238 at ε=1\varepsilon=1, dropping to 0.3180.318 at ε=5\varepsilon=5 as
NSRspur\operatorname{NSR}_{\mathrm{spur}} collapses below NSRcaus\operatorname{NSR}_{\mathrm{caus}} and inverts the
ranking. A single broken symmetry (β=[0,1,−0.4]\beta=[0,1,-0.4], satisfying
Assumption A2) recovers AUROC =1.000=1.000 with separation ratio =134=134.
The failure is geometric, not combinatorial.

Convergence rates. Fitted log-log slopes of −0.539-0.539 (H1H_{1}) and
−1.020-1.020 (H0H_{0}) confirm the Op​(n−1/2)O_{p}(n^{-1/2}) and Op​(n−1)O_{p}(n^{-1}) rates of
Theorem 4.2 to within 8%8\% and 2%2\%; the rate ratio grows as
n\sqrt{n} from 1.461.46 at n=100n=100 to 22.222.2 at n=25,000n=25{,}000. Full sweep in
Appendix A.8.

Weak-shift collapse. At K=5K=5, n=2,000n=2{,}000, the empirical NSR curve,
exact population prediction (Proposition 3), and
O​(ε4)O(\varepsilon^{4}) asymptotic agree to within 0.3%0.3\% for ε<0.13\varepsilon<0.13.
The empirical curve sits above population by 9.0×10−49.0\times 10^{-4} for
ε<0.2\varepsilon<0.2, consistent with the Op​(n−1)O_{p}(n^{-1}) floor of 1.1×10−31.1\times 10^{-3}. The predicted floor-exit ε∗=0.655\varepsilon^{*}=0.655 matches the observed
crossover at ε=0.74\varepsilon=0.74 to within 11%11\%. The three-curve overlay is
in Appendix A.8.
